stem:
A 33-year-old woman who had an episode of optic neuritis last year describes brief electric-shock sensations that shoot down her back and into both legs whenever she bends her head forward to read her phone. The sensation stops as soon as she lifts her head. Neurological examination today is normal.

Which named clinical phenomenon does this describe?
why_correct: Lhermitte sign is a brief electric-shock sensation running down the spine and limbs on neck flexion. It reflects irritability of demyelinated dorsal column pathways in the cervical cord and is classically described in multiple sclerosis, which fits her earlier optic neuritis. It can also occur with other cervical cord disease. Source: NICE CKS, Multiple sclerosis (clinical features), reviewed 2024.
why_wrong: A. Uhthoff phenomenon is temporary worsening of existing symptoms when body temperature rises, for example with a hot bath or fever. B. Romberg sign is loss of balance with the eyes closed, indicating impaired joint position sense. C. Tinel sign is tingling produced by tapping over an entrapped peripheral nerve, such as the median nerve at the wrist. E. Babinski response is an upgoing great toe on plantar stimulation and signals an upper motor neurone lesion.
pearl: Neck-flexion electric shocks in a young adult with previous optic neuritis should prompt thought of demyelination in the cervical cord.
thinking: Brief electric shock on neck flexion  ↓  cervical cord dorsal column irritability  ↓  Lhermitte sign  ↓  think multiple sclerosis (other cord disease possible).
exam_trap: Uhthoff phenomenon is also an MS eponym, but it is triggered by heat rather than by neck flexion.
takeaway: Electric-shock sensation down the spine on neck flexion is Lhermitte sign, a feature of cervical cord pathology such as multiple sclerosis.
notes: Re-angled from a bare eponym recall to a short clinical vignette with an MS clue; distractors changed (Uhthoff added, Murphy dropped). Clinical content carried over unchanged. No live PLAB 1 question tests Lhermitte sign (grep). Eponym itself not guideline-dependent; CKS cited generally, not re-fetched.

Skip: duplicates live BX169 (fluent nonsensical speech with impaired comprehension = Wernicke/receptive aphasia).

stem:
A 66-year-old man is chatting with friends in a cafe when he abruptly cannot find the words he wants. One friend notices that the corner of his mouth looks lower than usual. He is awake and clearly distressed, and the paramedics have just arrived.

What should the crew assume until a specialist assessment shows otherwise?

options.A: Migraine aura, with a headache expected to follow shortly
options.B: Acute stroke, needing immediate transfer to a stroke unit
options.C: A functional neurological disorder, needing calm reassurance
options.D: Early dementia with a gradual decline in language ability
options.E: Bell palsy, to be managed with oral steroids at home now

correct_answer: B. Acute stroke, needing immediate transfer to a stroke unit
why_correct: Sudden speech or language disturbance, especially with facial drooping, is a focal neurological deficit and should be treated as stroke or TIA until proven otherwise. NICE advises using a validated tool such as FAST (Face, Arm, Speech, Time) outside hospital for people with sudden-onset neurological symptoms, then rapid transfer for brain imaging so that time-critical treatment is not missed. Hypoglycaemia should also be excluded. Source: NICE NG128, Stroke and TIA in over 16s, 2022 update.
why_wrong: A. Migraine aura can cause transient language disturbance, but it spreads gradually, usually precedes headache and is a diagnosis of exclusion in a first sudden event. C. A functional disorder is only considered after organic causes are excluded and must never be assumed at presentation. D. Dementia declines over months to years, not abruptly. E. Bell palsy causes forehead-involving lower motor neurone weakness and does not cause word-finding difficulty.
pearl: A new focal deficit with a sudden start is a stroke or TIA until proven otherwise, and FAST is the community screen.
thinking: Sudden word-finding problem plus facial droop  ↓  FAST positive  ↓  assume stroke or TIA  ↓  emergency transfer for imaging and treatment decisions.
exam_trap: Reassuring alternatives such as migraine aura or Bell palsy delay treatment if the deficit is actually a stroke.
takeaway: Treat any sudden speech disturbance with facial droop as acute stroke until assessment proves otherwise.
notes: Re-angled to a community/paramedic FAST scenario. Merged learning point with PAN10578, PAN5161 and PAN539 (all sudden-onset stroke recognition), which are skipped. Distractors reworded; Alzheimer/primary progressive aphasia options replaced by dementia and Bell palsy. NG128 recs 1.1.1-1.1.3 re-fetched (FAST outside hospital, exclude hypoglycaemia, ROSIER in ED).
Skip: dysphasia/aphasia terminology is covered by live BX168/BX169; the dysarthria versus dysphasia distinction is taken by PAN3902 in this batch.

stem:
A 63-year-old man is recovering from a small brainstem stroke. His speech sounds slurred and mumbled, as though he had been drinking, although he has not. He chooses his words accurately, builds grammatically correct sentences and follows two-step commands without difficulty.

Which term best describes his speech problem?
why_correct: Dysarthria is impaired articulation of speech caused by weakness or incoordination of the muscles, or the neural pathways, that control the lips, tongue, palate and larynx. Language itself, meaning word choice, grammar and comprehension, is preserved. Brainstem and cerebellar lesions are common causes after stroke. Source: Royal College of Physicians, National Clinical Guideline for Stroke, 2023 (communication and swallowing).
why_wrong: B. Dysphasia is a disorder of language content or comprehension, which is intact here. C. Dysphonia is an abnormal voice quality, such as hoarseness, rather than slurred articulation. D. Dysmetria is inaccurate judgement of distance during limb movements. E. Apraxia of speech is a motor planning disorder with effortful, inconsistent sound errors and groping, so it is a less likely label when slurring is uniform.
pearl: Slurred speech with intact words and comprehension is dysarthria, not dysphasia.
thinking: Slurred speech  ↓  are word choice, grammar and comprehension normal?  ↓  yes: articulation problem  ↓  dysarthria.
exam_trap: Dysarthria (articulation) and dysphasia (language) are easily swapped because the names look similar.
takeaway: Dysarthria is impaired articulation with preserved language; dysphasia is impaired language.
notes: Dysarthria-versus-dysphasia distinction retained; recast with a stroke vignette. Merged PAN5578 (same point, skipped). Dysphagia and aphasia distractors replaced to avoid swallow/language confusion; apraxia of speech added. Terminology only, no guideline dependence; RCP guideline cited generally, not re-fetched.
Skip: duplicates live BX884 (aphasia as the cortical localising sign in sudden right arm weakness) and BX633.
Skip: duplicates live BX168 and PAQ15259 (Broca aphasia: effortful non-fluent speech, preserved comprehension).

stem:
A 75-year-old right-handed woman is brought in after her husband found that she could not follow any of his instructions. She talks freely in long, well-formed sentences that include invented words and make little sense. Her limb strength is normal. Imaging confirms a recent infarct.

In which area of the brain is the infarct most likely to lie?
why_correct: Fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension is receptive (Wernicke) aphasia. Wernicke area lies in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the language-dominant hemisphere, which is the left in almost all right-handed people. Because the motor cortex is spared, limb strength is often normal. Source: Royal College of Physicians, National Clinical Guideline for Stroke, 2023 (communication disorders); standard neuroanatomy.
why_wrong: A. The left inferior frontal gyrus is Broca area, whose damage gives effortful non-fluent speech with preserved comprehension. B. The right parietal lobe is associated with neglect and visuospatial problems rather than language loss. C. The left occipital lobe supplies the right visual field and does not produce fluent nonsensical speech. D. The cerebellar vermis affects truncal balance and gait, not language.
pearl: Fluent nonsense plus poor comprehension points to the dominant temporal lobe, whereas non-fluent speech points to the frontal lobe.
thinking: Fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension  ↓  Wernicke aphasia  ↓  dominant (left) posterior superior temporal gyrus.
exam_trap: Choosing the frontal lobe because speech is the main complaint ignores that fluency and comprehension separate temporal from frontal lesions.
takeaway: Wernicke aphasia localises to the language-dominant posterior temporal region; Broca aphasia localises to the inferior frontal gyrus.
notes: Learning point is lesion localisation of Wernicke aphasia (live BX169 asks for the aphasia type, not the location; PAQ15259 covers Broca location only). Source distractors reworded; right-handed specified so dominant side is unambiguous. Established neuroanatomy, not re-fetched.
Skip: duplicates live NEU048 and NEU068 (sudden right-sided weakness with aphasia in acute stroke: urgent imaging/thrombolysis); NEU004 and ACU018 also cover this.
Skip: duplicates live BX168/BX169 (aphasia as language deficit); aphasia terminology already tested.
Skip: same learning point as PAN3902 in this batch (dysarthria = articulation problem with preserved language).
Skip: sudden-onset focal deficit as the hallmark of stroke is tested by live NEU004/NEU007/NEU048 and covered in this batch by PAN1256; avoids repeating the point.
Skip: duplicates live BX878 (aphasia with right arm weakness = left hemisphere) and BX627.
Skip: duplicates live BX168 (speech production difficulty with preserved comprehension = expressive aphasia).

stem:
A 71-year-old woman is medically stable four days after an ischaemic stroke and is on the acute stroke unit. She has left-sided weakness, needs help to wash, dress and move from bed to chair, and is anxious about going home. Her family ask what her recovery plan should be.

What is the most appropriate approach to her rehabilitation?

options.A: Individualised rehabilitation with goals agreed by a multidisciplinary stroke team
options.B: Postpone all therapy until she is able to stand and walk unaided on the ward
options.C: Advise prolonged bed rest in the first weeks to protect her neurological recovery
options.D: Provide a printed exercise sheet and rely on her family to supervise at home
options.E: Arrange outpatient physiotherapy alone, starting only after discharge from hospital

correct_answer: A. Individualised rehabilitation with goals agreed by a multidisciplinary stroke team
why_correct: Stroke rehabilitation should be delivered by a multidisciplinary team (for example physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, nursing and psychology) and tailored to the person's needs and agreed goals. It should start once the person is medically stable and continue after discharge, for example through early supported discharge or community stroke teams, for as long as it helps them meet those goals. Source: NICE NG236, Stroke rehabilitation in adults, 2023.
why_wrong: B. Waiting until she can walk unaided loses the period when recovery is greatest and leaves problems with self-care and communication untreated. C. Prolonged bed rest causes deconditioning, pressure injury and venous thromboembolism and is not recommended. D. A leaflet plus family supervision does not provide skilled assessment or goal-setting and ignores her need for occupational therapy and other disciplines. E. Starting only after discharge leaves a gap in care and misses early inpatient therapy.
pearl: Rehabilitation after stroke is a team activity that starts early and follows individual goals, not a single profession or a single setting.
thinking: Stable after stroke with functional deficits  ↓  assess needs across disciplines  ↓  set individual goals with patient and family  ↓  MDT rehabilitation, continuing in the community.
exam_trap: Offering physiotherapy alone, or leaving everything until discharge, ignores the multidisciplinary and early nature of stroke rehabilitation.
takeaway: After stroke, offer early, multidisciplinary rehabilitation tailored to the person's needs and goals.
notes: Vignette expanded; options reworded (source distractors 'physiotherapy without OT' and 'home exercise leaflet' merged into new wording). NG236 (2023) section 1.1 re-fetched: MDT roles, continuing rehab as long as it helps achieve goals, early supported discharge. No numeric threshold used; deliberately avoided claims about very early high-dose mobilisation.
Skip: duplicates live NEU105, NEU041 and NEU002 (sudden severe headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds, subarachnoid haemorrhage); NEU105 has a nearly identical scenario.
